newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Southern Africa sees 16 pct fall in '97 maize crop.
newsitem.headline: Southern Africa sees 16 pct fall in '97 maize crop.

text.p: Southern Africa could see a 16 percent fall in production of its staple maize crop this year due to floods in some states and severe drought in others, the Southern African Development Community (SADC) said on Tuesday.

SADC's Food Security Unit forecast in its latest regional report for the 12 southern African countries that 1996/97 maize production might drop 16 percent to 17,142 million tonnes from the previous season.
The forecast excluded cereal production in SADC's newest member, Mauritius.
Total cereal production for the region -- including wheat, rice and millet -- was forecast at 22.61 million tonnes, down from 26.81 million tonnes in the 1995/96 season.

The unit blamed excessive rains and flooding in South Africa, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Zambia and Malawi coupled with dry spells and a late start to rains in South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho for the projected decline in output.
In addition, the region's third-largest producer, Tanzania has been suffering from severe drought and could produce 2.1 million tonnes -- down 20 percent on the 1995/96 production season.

"Indications are that the final regional forecast may fall even lower given that some countries, notably Malawi and Namibia which are yet to finalise their forecasts, may come up with reduced estimates," the unit said.
It said the region -- which includes some of the poorest countries in the world according to the World Bank -- could face a serious cereal shortage in the 1997/98 marketing year.
"The SADC region is projected as facing an overall cereal shortfall of 2.3 million tonnes during the ensuing 1997/98 marketing year in which all cereal crops are likely to be in short supply."
Maize production alone is predicted to fall short by some 783,000 tonnes.
SADC said this compared unfavourably with a regional surplus of 1.79 million tonnes in the previous marketing year.
"Maize shortfalls of varying magnitudes are forecast in the other SADC countries," the community said.
The Food Security Unit report said exportable maize surpluses could only be expected in SADC's two largest producers -- South Africa and Zimbabwe in the 1996/97 season.
But even then, South Africa's exports will be severely cut to 587,000 this year from last year's 2.3 million tonnes.
SADC estimated South Africa's 1996/97 maize crop to be 8.21 million tonnes -- a 17 percent decrease on the previous season.
Zimbabwe, the second largest producer after South Africa, could see a 2.195 million tonnes crop, 16 percent down on the 1995/96 season.

Namibia is expected to increase its 1996/97 maize crop by 161 percent to 47,000 tonnes and Mozambique -- still recovering from a 16-year civil war which all but destroyed its economy -- should produce 10 percent more maize than last year. SADC expected Mozambique to produce 1.043 million tonnes.
The regional grouping comprises Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Zambia, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Tanzania, Zimbabwe and Mauritius.
